dataset.input:
EXCERPT from the Constitutional Court of South Africa judgment in S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC):

'In my view, section 11(2) of the Constitution prohibits the death penalty. The right to life is the most fundamental of all rights. The death penalty extinguishes this right in a final and irreversible manner. While the state has a legitimate interest in punishing crime, capital punishment constitutes a cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment within the meaning of section 11(2). The limitation clause (section 33) cannot save it because the death penalty cannot be justified in an open and democratic society based on freedom and equality.

It may be that some members of the public support the death penalty. However, the question before us is not what the majority of South Africans believe, but what the Constitution requires. The Constitution is the supreme law and its values — human dignity, equality, and freedom — must guide our interpretation.

Ubuntu is a value that informs our constitutional framework. It emphasises communality and the interdependence of the members of a community. It recognises a person's status as a human being, entitled to unconditional respect, dignity, value, and acceptance. The death penalty is fundamentally inconsistent with Ubuntu.'

Based on this excerpt, identify: (1) the three independent grounds on which the court found the death penalty unconstitutional; (2) how the limitation clause analysis was applied; and (3) the role Ubuntu played in the court's reasoning.
dataset.target:
(1) Three independent grounds: (a) the death penalty violates the right to life (section 9 of the interim Constitution; section 11 of the final Constitution); (b) the death penalty constitutes cruel, inhuman, and degrading punishment under section 11(2); (c) the death penalty cannot be justified under the limitation clause. Each ground independently renders the death penalty unconstitutional.

(2) Limitation clause analysis: The court applied a two-stage test: (a) whether the death penalty limits a right in the Bill of Rights (yes — both the right to life and the right to freedom from cruel punishment); (b) whether the limitation is justifiable in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality, and freedom (no — the death penalty is disproportionate, irreversible, and inconsistent with constitutional values). The court rejected the argument that the state's interest in deterrence justified the limitation.

(3) Role of Ubuntu: The court referenced Ubuntu as a foundational constitutional value that reinforces the conclusion that the death penalty is unconstitutional. Ubuntu was not the ratio decidendi but served as a hermeneutic value — a prism through which the Constitution's commitment to human dignity and communality must be understood. It did not replace the legal analysis but enriched it. This aspect became binding as an interpretive principle for future cases.

dataset.input:
EXCERPT from the Constitutional Court of South Africa judgment in Barkhuizen v Napier 2007 (5) SA 323 (CC):

'The applicant contends that the time-bar clause in his insurance policy, which requires that any claim be brought within 30 days, is contrary to public policy and therefore unenforceable. The question before this court is what test should be applied to determine whether a contractual term is contrary to public policy in the constitutional era.

Public policy is now rooted in the Constitution and the fundamental values it enshrines, including human dignity, equality, and freedom. Pacta sunt servanda (agreements must be kept) is itself a manifestation of these constitutional values — it gives effect to the freedom and dignity of parties who voluntarily enter into contracts. However, where a contractual term is manifestly unfair, unjust, or unreasonable to the extent that it offends constitutional values, a court may refuse to enforce it.

This requires a two-stage enquiry. First, is the clause itself contrary to public policy when considered in abstract? A clause will be contrary to public policy if it is manifestly unfair or unreasonable. Second, even if the clause is not contrary to public policy per se, would its enforcement in the particular circumstances of the case be contrary to public policy? This second stage requires a consideration of all relevant circumstances, including the relative bargaining positions of the parties.

The present case is remitted to the High Court for determination on the second stage. We express no view on whether the 30-day time-bar in this particular policy passes constitutional muster in the specific circumstances of this case.'

Based on this excerpt, what is the two-stage test the Constitutional Court established, and why did the court remit the case rather than decide it?
dataset.target:
The two-stage test: (1) Objective stage — is the contractual clause itself contrary to public policy? The court considers whether the clause is 'manifestly unfair, unjust, or unreasonable' when viewed in abstract, applying constitutional values of dignity, equality, and freedom. (2) Contextual stage — would enforcement of the clause in the particular circumstances of the case be contrary to public policy? This requires examining the specific facts, including the parties' relative bargaining power, the circumstances under which the contract was concluded, and the consequences of enforcement.

The court remitted the case because the High Court had not made factual findings on the second stage. The Constitutional Court is a court of constitutional review — it decides constitutional principles and remits factual disputes to the trial court for determination. The Constitutional Court expressed no view on whether the 30-day time-bar was enforceable in this specific case because it lacked the necessary factual findings on issues such as whether the applicant was aware of the clause, whether the applicant could have negotiated different terms, and whether enforcement would be unconscionable in the circumstances.
